Story: Package and publish the MOSAIC Cloud Run image
Outcome: Produce a reproducible container image that follows the Cloud Run container contract without embedding environment configuration or credentials.
Implementation notes: Update the Dockerfile and CI pipeline to start the MOSAIC-owned bootstrap, run as a non-root user, listen on the PORT environment variable and publish the image to Artifact Registry. Record the immutable image digest used by Terraform. Keep the capability snapshot, database credentials and Git credentials outside the image.
Acceptance criteria: The image builds in CI; starts locally with a configurable port; starts on Cloud Run using PORT; runs as a non-root user; is published to the approved Artifact Registry repository; Terraform consumes an immutable digest; image inspection finds no environment credentials or capability snapshot.

Story: Provision the Release 1 Cloud SQL database
Outcome: Provide one durable PostgreSQL database per environment for ADK sessions and MOSAIC application metadata.
Implementation notes: Use Terraform to provision Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, the environment database, service identities and least-privilege connectivity for the Cloud Run service and administrator Job. Use workload identity where supported and Secret Manager for any database credential the client library still requires. Define separate ADK and MOSAIC schemas or collision-free table namespaces. Do not import SQLite data.
Acceptance criteria: Terraform creates one environment database; the Cloud Run service and administrator Job connect without a public credential in source control; unauthorised identities cannot connect; ADK and MOSAIC namespaces do not collide; a clean database can be recreated without data migration; production HA and restore targets remain explicitly out of scope.

Story: Deploy and configure MOSAIC on Cloud Run
Outcome: Make the ADA deployment path repeatable, reviewable and reversible for Release 1.
Implementation notes: Create Terraform for the Cloud Run service using the approved image digest and service identity. Configure Cloud SQL attachment, environment variables, Secret Manager references, CPU and memory, instance-based billing so background work can continue after an SSE disconnect, minimum and maximum instances of one for the pilot, request timeout, startup probe and structured logging. Force a new revision when the image or configuration hash changes and document rollback to the previous healthy revision.
Acceptance criteria: A Terraform apply deploys a healthy revision; configuration is supplied outside the image; background invocation work continues after the client disconnects while the instance remains alive; SSE can remain open for the documented timeout; a changed image or configuration creates a revision; failed readiness prevents traffic; rollback restores the previous healthy revision; instance termination may interrupt in-flight work and never resumes it.

Story: Publish the capability snapshot through GCS
Outcome: Deliver the approved JSON configuration to Cloud Run without embedding it in the image.
Implementation notes: Commit capability-runtime-snapshot.json as a standalone file in the private Terraform environment configuration. Have Terraform upload a content-addressed or versioned object to a restricted GCS bucket, mount the bucket read-only in Cloud Run, set MOSAIC_CAPABILITY_RUNTIME_SNAPSHOT_PATH and pass a content hash that causes a new revision when the file changes.
Acceptance criteria: Terraform uploads the reviewed file and grants read access only to the runtime identity; the Cloud Run revision sees it at the configured path; changing the JSON changes the revision hash; the image contains no copy; the object contains no credentials; startup rejects a missing, malformed, oversized or inconsistent snapshot through the existing validator.

Story: Seed the read-only pilot capability configuration
Outcome: Provide every endpoint, provider tool, target, capability and binding required by the agreed development pilot scenarios.
Implementation notes: Populate the committed snapshot using the existing schema and validator. Include only development endpoints and read-only provider tools. Keep credentials outside the file. Add a CI command that executes the same whole-snapshot validation used at MOSAIC startup.
Acceptance criteria: Every pilot Skill resolves to valid bindings; every binding uses an approved provider/tool pair; write-capable tools are absent; CI rejects malformed or inconsistent snapshots; MOSAIC starts successfully with the approved file and fails clearly with a deliberately invalid fixture.

Story: Load only approved Skills from the configured branch
Outcome: Keep the current Git catalogue mechanism while making Cloud Run startup and publication behaviour explicit.
Implementation notes: Use the existing configurable catalogue branch and set it to main. Treat merge to main as publication approval. Clone into Cloud Run temporary storage during startup, obtaining any private Git credential from Secret Manager. Validate Skill packages and mosaic.yaml bindings against the capability snapshot. Do not add tag or commit pinning.
Acceptance criteria: A clean Cloud Run revision loads main; no writable or persistent catalogue filesystem is required; invalid Skill packages or missing bindings fail startup clearly; only atomic Skill IDs reach the workspace service; reverting a catalogue commit and deploying a revision restores the previous catalogue.

Story: Expose only supported pilot routes and streaming
Outcome: Publish Dash and /api/v1 on Cloud Run while preventing public use of raw ADA and development routes.
Implementation notes: Set WEB_ENABLED=false. Apply the ADA platform ingress pattern and an outer route allowlist so only the Dash root, Dash assets and callbacks, sign-in, /api/v1 and required health probes reach handlers. Deny /run, /run_sse, /run_live, raw session, builder, debug, test and eval paths before ADA processes them. Preserve forwarded headers and configure the end-to-end timeout for SSE. Do not enable WebSockets.
Acceptance criteria: Supported paths work through the Cloud Run URL or approved load balancer; raw ADA/ADK and development paths receive the documented denial; startup and health probes succeed without becoming general public APIs; an SSE response remains open for the configured timeout and streams incrementally; WebSocket support is absent.

Story: Configure ADK sessions on Cloud SQL
Outcome: Persist complete ADK event history and session state outside Cloud Run instances.
Implementation notes: Configure ADA/ADK to construct its supported database-backed SessionService with the Release 1 PostgreSQL URI instead of the development SQLite default. Use the agreed ADK schema or table namespace and preserve keys by app_name, user_id and session_id. Apply ADK initialisation through the supported startup or migration path without changing ADK session models.
Acceptance criteria: A clean database creates the ADK tables; completed conversations survive Cloud Run instance and revision replacement; a user cannot list or reopen another user's sessions through the wrapper API; startup fails readiness when the database is unavailable; no session.db file is used in the deployed service.

Story: Create the MOSAIC PostgreSQL foundation
Outcome: Give MOSAIC an application-owned schema that is independent of ADK session tables.
Implementation notes: Declare SQLAlchemy, a PostgreSQL driver and Alembic as direct dependencies. Add the configured database URL, a MOSAIC schema or collision-free table prefix, connection pool and session factory. Create a baseline migration. Run migrations through a Cloud Run Job before service rollout, not independently in every service instance. Use application-generated UUIDs and portable SQLAlchemy types.
Acceptance criteria: A blank environment database produces the MOSAIC schema; rerunning the migration Job is idempotent; a failed migration prevents rollout; MOSAIC code never modifies ADK-owned tables; local development may use SQLite but the deployed Cloud Run service uses PostgreSQL only.

Story: Persist pilot users and access tokens
Outcome: Store stable human user identities and revocable token credentials without retaining plaintext tokens.
Implementation notes: Add users and access_tokens models, migrations and repository methods. A user_id is unique and immutable. Token rows contain an application-generated token ID, SHA-256 hash, status, created_at, disabled_at and rotated_at. Enforce foreign keys and indexes required for token lookup.
Acceptance criteria: Duplicate user_id values are rejected; plaintext tokens never enter the database; disabling a user or token prevents successful lookup; token rotation leaves only the new token active; repository tests cover enabled, disabled, missing and duplicate records.

Story: Persist one workspace and atomic Skill references per user
Outcome: Keep Skill selection outside session state and make it available to every conversation owned by the user.
Implementation notes: Add workspaces and workspace_skills models, migrations and a service layer. Create one workspace automatically with the user. Store only atomic Skill IDs, a workspace version and timestamps. Replace a Skill set in one transaction and reject duplicate references. Do not store Skill definitions or group references.
Acceptance criteria: Every user has exactly one workspace; a new workspace starts with no Skills; replacing the set is atomic; duplicate IDs do not produce duplicate rows; removing a Skill reference does not alter the catalogue; concurrent stale updates fail rather than silently overwriting a newer version.

Story: Run administrator user commands as a Cloud Run Job
Outcome: Let an authorised platform administrator create, inspect, disable and rotate pilot credentials without an administration UI or container shell.
Implementation notes: Add mosaic-admin users create, list, disable and rotate-token commands. Define an on-demand Cloud Run Job using the same image, runtime identity, Cloud SQL attachment and configuration as the service, with a command override for mosaic-admin. Generate at least 256 bits of randomness with a mosaic_r1_ prefix. Print plaintext only once to the invoking terminal and never store or log it.
Acceptance criteria: An authorised administrator can execute the documented Job with command arguments; create returns one usable token and creates an empty workspace transactionally; list never prints token material; disable takes effect on the next request; rotation immediately rejects the previous token; unauthorised users cannot execute the Job; duplicate user creation exits non-zero with a clear message.

Story: Provide administrator commands for workspace Skills
Outcome: Allow pilot Skill assignments through the administrator Cloud Run Job without building a catalogue or workspace-management UI.
Implementation notes: Add mosaic-admin workspaces show-skills and set-skills. Accept repeated --skill and --group options. Load and validate against the same Public catalogue configuration as the service, expand a group to its current atomic members and store only the resulting atomic references. Require an explicit --clear option for an empty set.
Acceptance criteria: Unknown or unpublished Skills are rejected without changing the workspace; group expansion is displayed through dry-run output; set-skills atomically replaces the set; show-skills lists stable IDs; later group changes do not alter existing workspace references; the commands run through the configured administrator Job.

Story: Authenticate bearer tokens at the outer ASGI boundary
Outcome: Establish a trusted user identity before any Dash, MOSAIC API or ADA route executes.
Implementation notes: Implement outermost ASGI middleware that accepts Authorization: Bearer for API calls, hashes the opaque token and resolves an enabled user. Attach an immutable trusted user context to the request. Apply authentication to every externally reachable application path, with narrowly listed exceptions for sign-in and internal health probes.
Acceptance criteria: Valid enabled tokens resolve the correct user; missing, malformed, disabled and rotated tokens return the same generic 401 shape; authentication runs before existing ADA middleware and routes; no request body, path or header other than the validated credential can establish user identity.

Story: Add browser token sign-in and sign-out
Outcome: Let pilot users authenticate through the web application without exposing the token to Dash client code.
Implementation notes: Implement POST /api/v1/auth/token and POST /api/v1/auth/logout. After validation, store the token in a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie with a configurable lifetime that defaults to seven days. Clear the cookie on sign-out. Support the same-origin deployment only.
Acceptance criteria: The browser can authenticate by pasting a token; JavaScript cannot read the cookie; the cookie survives a browser restart until expiry; logout clears it; disabled or rotated tokens fail even when an old cookie remains; production mode refuses to issue a non-Secure cookie.

Story: Enforce trusted identity on wrapper requests
Outcome: Prevent an authenticated pilot user from impersonating another user through ADA-compatible request fields.
Implementation notes: Create a request-context dependency used by every /api/v1 handler. Set app_name and user_id server-side. Reject or ignore caller-supplied user_id, workspace ID and ownership state. Pass only the derived identity into the ADA invocation and session service adapters.
Acceptance criteria: Changing user_id or workspace fields in a request never changes ownership; logs record the derived user ID; wrapper handlers cannot be called without the trusted context dependency; automated tests cover body, query, path and header spoof attempts.

Story: Standardise authentication failure behaviour
Outcome: Return predictable failures without leaking token, user or route details.
Implementation notes: Define 401 and 403 response envelopes with correlation_id, stable error code and concise action. Add tests across bearer, cookie, disabled-user and expired-cookie paths. Ensure access logs redact Authorization and Cookie headers.
Acceptance criteria: All authentication failures use the documented envelope; no response or log contains a token or token hash; an expired cookie prompts sign-in; API clients receive a machine-readable code; correlation IDs match the server log entry.

Story: Define the supported /api/v1 conversation contract
Outcome: Give Dash and direct human API clients one stable interface that hides raw ADA routes.
Implementation notes: Define OpenAPI models for create/list/get conversation, submit message, read invocation status and cancel invocation. Define SSE event names, correlation headers and error envelopes. Use conversation as the public term while mapping it to an ADK session internally.
Acceptance criteria: The generated OpenAPI document contains no raw ADA request models; all routes require the trusted user dependency; examples cover bearer and cookie authentication; error models include 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 and 500; the contract is versioned under /api/v1.

Story: Create, list and reopen owned conversations
Outcome: Allow a user to navigate persistent ADK sessions without duplicating conversation data in MOSAIC tables.
Implementation notes: Implement POST and GET /api/v1/conversations plus GET /api/v1/conversations/{conversation_id}. Generate conversation IDs server-side. Read and write through ADK SessionService using the trusted app_name and user_id. Derive the display title from a truncated first user prompt and return created_at and last_activity_at.
Acceptance criteria: A new conversation belongs to the authenticated user; lists contain only that user's conversations ordered by recent activity; reopening returns complete persisted history; titles require no extra model call; unknown and foreign IDs return the same 404 response.

Story: Stream an invocation through the supported API
Outcome: Deliver model and orchestration events progressively to browser and API clients.
Implementation notes: Implement POST /api/v1/conversations/{id}/messages as an SSE response backed by the existing ADA execution path. Override app_name and user_id from trusted context. Translate ADA events into the documented public event types without exposing internal state, raw provider payloads or stack traces.
Acceptance criteria: Text events can be rendered incrementally; terminal completed and failed events are always emitted when the connection remains open; the endpoint works with cookie and bearer authentication; forwarded identity is trusted; SSE headers prevent buffering and caching.

Story: Continue an invocation after browser disconnection
Outcome: Persist a completed response even when the initiating browser closes or loses its SSE connection.
Implementation notes: Run each invocation as an application-owned background asyncio task keyed by conversation and invocation ID. Let SSE subscribers observe the task without owning its lifetime. Persist resulting ADK events normally. Expose status through GET /api/v1/conversations/{id}/invocations/current. Keep the registry in memory because Release 1 has one replica.
Acceptance criteria: Dropping the SSE client does not cancel the task; reopening the conversation after completion shows the final response; reopening during execution returns working status; Cloud Run instance termination marks the in-memory invocation interrupted and does not resume it; completed tasks are removed from the registry.

Story: Prevent overlapping work in one conversation
Outcome: Avoid concurrent mutations of the same ADK session without adding a queue.
Implementation notes: Acquire an in-process guard for the conversation before creating an invocation. When a task is already active, return HTTP 409 with the conversation ID, stable error code and exact explanation. Release the guard on every terminal path, including failure and cancellation.
Acceptance criteria: Only one task can run for a conversation; separate conversations can run concurrently; conflicting requests are never queued; the 409 response does not use vague retry language; failure and cancellation do not leave a stale lock.

Story: Cancel an active invocation explicitly
Outcome: Let a user terminate work and then submit a different prompt without resuming abandoned execution.
Implementation notes: Implement POST /api/v1/conversations/{id}/invocations/current/cancel. Verify conversation ownership, request cancellation from the invocation manager and call the owner-provided orchestration cancellation hook. Persist a terminal cancelled event and discard late events from cancelled work.
Acceptance criteria: Only the owner can cancel; repeated cancellation is idempotent; cancelled work is never resumed; the per-conversation guard is released only after terminal cancellation; the next prompt can start normally; cancelling a completed or unknown invocation returns the documented result.

Story: Create the Python Dash application shell
Outcome: Provide a maintainable Python-based web application within the existing FastAPI process.
Implementation notes: Create a Dash application that uses the existing FastAPI backend and is registered through an extension function called by the MOSAIC bootstrap. Add local CSS and JavaScript assets, application layout, navigation container and error boundary. Do not add a production Node.js server or WebSocket dependency.
Acceptance criteria: The application loads at / through Cloud Run; Dash callbacks and assets work under the configured paths; the module can be tested without starting the orchestrator; no Goal, routing or provider logic exists in the UI package.

Story: Build token sign-in and sign-out screens
Outcome: Allow an invited pilot user to establish and clear the persistent browser authentication cookie.
Implementation notes: Build a token-entry form that calls /api/v1/auth/token and never stores the token in dcc.Store, localStorage, sessionStorage, URLs or analytics. Redirect authenticated users to conversations. Add sign-out and clear client state after logout.
Acceptance criteria: A valid token signs in; invalid or disabled tokens show the generic API message; page reload and browser restart remain signed in until cookie expiry; sign-out returns to the token screen; front-end logs and browser storage contain no token.

Story: Navigate persistent conversations
Outcome: Let the user start a conversation and reopen their previous conversations.
Implementation notes: Create a sidebar that lists title, created time and last activity. Add New conversation and selection behaviour. Load conversation history through /api/v1 only. Preserve the selected conversation during ordinary page updates and show an empty state for a new user.
Acceptance criteria: The list is ordered by recent activity; creating a conversation selects it; reopening renders its persisted history; foreign conversations cannot be displayed; empty and API-failure states are understandable; deletion, renaming and sharing controls are absent.

Story: Render chat and consume SSE with client-side JavaScript
Outcome: Display response text while it is generated without introducing a React source project or WebSockets.
Implementation notes: Build the chat transcript and composer in Dash. Add a small local JavaScript module that submits the prompt with fetch, parses the SSE stream and batches updates into a Dash component or dcc.Store through dash_clientside.set_props. Render Markdown with raw HTML disabled. Use cookie authentication automatically.
Acceptance criteria: User text appears immediately; response text grows as events arrive; batching keeps the interface responsive; Markdown cannot execute HTML or scripts; a completed event finalises the message; stream parsing tests cover split chunks, multiple events and malformed events.

Story: Show pilot runtime states and cancellation
Outcome: Make active, waiting, completed, cancelled and failed interactions clear without exposing internal orchestration stages.
Implementation notes: Show a busy indicator while an invocation runs and disable Send for that conversation. Add Cancel, calling the supported endpoint rather than only aborting fetch. Display awaiting-user-input, completed, cancelled and failed states. Show correlation IDs on errors. On reconnection, query current status and reload persisted history.
Acceptance criteria: One conversation cannot submit overlapping prompts; cancellation reaches a terminal state before Send is enabled; closing the page does not send cancellation; reopening shows working or completed state; errors contain an actionable message and correlation ID but no raw provider data.

Story: Test and polish the pilot interface
Outcome: Deliver a usable internal pilot interface across supported desktop browser sizes.
Implementation notes: Add automated tests for sign-in, conversation navigation, stream updates, cancellation and failure states. Add keyboard labels, visible focus states, sensible colour contrast and responsive layout for common laptop widths. Keep styling local and self-hosted.
Acceptance criteria: Critical user journeys pass in CI; primary controls are keyboard reachable and labelled; text remains readable at supported widths; no asset depends on an external CDN; the interface does not expose deferred Skill-management or administration controls.

Story: Own the MOSAIC FastAPI bootstrap
Outcome: Create the controlled extension point that lets non-orchestrator modules reuse ADA's FastAPI application.
Implementation notes: Add a MOSAIC-owned entrypoint that calls ada_sdk.api.base_api.create_app(), registers the outer route and authentication middleware, /api/v1 routers and Dash extension, then starts Uvicorn on the PORT environment variable with a local default. Change the container entrypoint to this module. Keep orchestration construction unchanged.
Acceptance criteria: Existing ADA and MOSAIC runtime behaviour still starts; registration order places route and authentication controls outermost; developer-owned modules are imported through explicit extension functions; raw routes remain available only behind the internal application boundary; no developer team is assigned this story.

Story: Provide terminal invocation cancellation
Outcome: Give the access layer a supported way to stop active orchestration without resuming it later.
Implementation notes: Expose an owner-controlled cancellation hook for the active invocation. Mark cancellation terminal, stop accepting further capability outcomes for that invocation, and make late task results unusable. Do not add Goal resumption or automatic topic-change detection.
Acceptance criteria: The access layer can request cancellation by invocation ID; cancelled work cannot transition back to active or completed; late results do not enter a later Goal; existing successful and failed terminal behaviour remains unchanged.

Story: Resolve workspace Skills at each new Goal
Outcome: Replace session-ID profile assignment as the normal pilot binding and keep an in-flight Goal stable.
Implementation notes: At the new-Goal boundary, read the authenticated user's atomic Skill references through the MOSAIC workspace service, validate them against the loaded catalogue and snapshot the resolved Skill set into Goal state. Do not accept Skill state supplied by the caller. Do not re-resolve during the same Goal.
Acceptance criteria: A user receives only their configured Skills; a withdrawn Skill is unavailable and cannot execute; an administrator change affects the next Goal, including a later Goal in the same conversation; an in-flight or clarification-held Goal keeps its original set; missing workspace Skills grant nothing.

Story: Verify authentication and conversation isolation
Outcome: Prove that two pilot users cannot read, continue, stream or cancel each other's conversations.
Implementation notes: Create integration tests using two enabled users, two tokens and separate workspaces. Exercise list, get, message, status and cancel endpoints with correct and incorrect ownership. Include body and header identity-spoof attempts and disabled-token cases.
Acceptance criteria: All cross-user operations return the documented non-disclosing error; same-user operations succeed; direct bearer and browser-cookie paths are covered; logs contain correlation and trusted user IDs but no credential material.

Story: Verify persistence across Cloud Run instance replacement
Outcome: Demonstrate the exact persistence promised by the Cloud SQL-backed pilot design.
Implementation notes: Provision a user and Skills, complete a conversation, then deploy a replacement Cloud Run revision or force an instance replacement. Authenticate again and reopen the conversation. Confirm that no local container filesystem is required and that an interrupted in-flight invocation is not resumed.
Acceptance criteria: User, token hash, workspace Skill references and completed ADK history survive Cloud Run instance and revision replacement; in-flight work may terminate and never resumes; a clean environment database can be initialised without importing SQLite data; evidence records the revision and database used.

Story: Verify the read-only pilot investigation
Outcome: Run the agreed platform scenarios using only approved development endpoints and the assigned workspace Skills.
Implementation notes: Execute at least one complete investigation for each seeded platform area. Include a user without the required Skill, a withdrawn or unknown Skill reference, provider denial and provider failure. Capture expected results without storing sensitive payloads in the test evidence.
Acceptance criteria: Assigned Skills enable the intended read-only capabilities; unassigned Skills grant nothing; no write-capable provider tool is invoked; denials and failures return bounded user messages with correlation IDs; the successful result remains in conversation history.

Story: Add pilot health, logging and operating instructions
Outcome: Give platform administrators enough information to operate and reset the development pilot.
Implementation notes: Add startup and readiness behaviour for configuration validation and database connectivity. Use structured logs with correlation_id, trusted user_id, conversation_id and invocation_id while excluding prompts, responses, tokens and raw capability data from new access logs. Add a Release 1 Cloud Run pilot runbook section to README.md.
Acceptance criteria: The runbook covers Terraform rollout and rollback, migration and administrator Jobs, token rotation or disablement, Skill assignment, GCS snapshot updates, log lookup and clean database initialisation; readiness fails on invalid configuration or unavailable database; correlation IDs locate one log trail.

Story: Complete the Release 1 acceptance walkthrough
Outcome: Produce one repeatable demonstration that proves the agreed pilot boundary and exclusions.
Implementation notes: Run the documented deployment and onboarding process from a clean development environment. Demonstrate sign-in, assigned Skills, live streaming, busy state, browser disconnect and completed reopen, explicit cancellation, direct human API access and Cloud Run revision replacement. Record defects and rerun failed criteria.
Acceptance criteria: Every Release 1 acceptance criterion is marked passed with evidence or explicitly rejected from release; the MOSAIC owner accepts ORCH-R1 behaviour; deferred capabilities are not presented as pilot features; the final known-limitations list matches the README.

Story: Integrate browser OIDC
Outcome: Replace pasted human tokens with organisational sign-in.
Implementation notes: Validate issuer, audience, signature and required claims; map the stable subject to a MOSAIC user; retain the current trusted request context.
Acceptance criteria: Interactive sign-in and logout work; invalid tokens fail closed; existing workspaces map to stable subjects; raw identity claims are not trusted outside the auth module.

Story: Retire development human tokens
Outcome: Remove the Release 1 token entry path after OIDC adoption.
Implementation notes: Disable token issuance and cookie exchange by environment flag; migrate administrative access procedures; remove token UI without changing API identity context.
Acceptance criteria: Production rejects development tokens; pilot environments can retain them only when explicitly enabled; documentation and tests use OIDC.

Story: Introduce independent service identities
Outcome: Support unattended API calls without impersonating human users.
Implementation notes: Define separate service identity records, credentials, scopes, workspace ownership and session semantics. Authenticate through the approved workload or OAuth mechanism rather than human cookies.
Acceptance criteria: Service calls are attributable to the service; they cannot use a human identity; credential rotation and disablement work; service sessions and policies are independently testable.

Story: Support coordinated multiple Cloud Run instances
Outcome: Remove the single-instance and in-memory invocation constraints while retaining Cloud SQL persistence.
Implementation notes: Move active invocation coordination and per-conversation locking to a shared mechanism supported by the production architecture. Exercise concurrent ADK session updates through PostgreSQL and route status or cancellation requests to the active worker or shared coordinator.
Acceptance criteria: Multiple Cloud Run instances serve requests without duplicate active work in one conversation; disconnect, status and cancellation work across instances; deployment rollout overlap is safe; load tests meet the agreed production target.

Story: Expose the Public Skill catalogue API
Outcome: Let authenticated users discover Public Skills and hierarchy through supported APIs.
Implementation notes: Return stable Skill IDs, display name, description, platform hierarchy, status and read-only classification from the validated catalogue. Do not expose provider credentials or internal paths.
Acceptance criteria: All Public Skills are visible; withdrawn Skills are marked unavailable; hierarchy queries return current atomic members; pagination and search are documented.

Story: Allow users to manage workspace Skills
Outcome: Replace administrator-only Skill assignment with safe self-service.
Implementation notes: Add versioned add/remove/bulk-group endpoints that validate Public Skills and update atomic references. Group selection expands current membership and creates no ongoing subscription.
Acceptance criteria: Users can change only their workspace; duplicates are idempotent; stale versions return conflict; adding a group stores atomic IDs; future group changes do not alter the workspace.

Story: Build Skill discovery and selection UI
Outcome: Let users understand, search and select Public Skills and hierarchy groups.
Implementation notes: Add catalogue pages, description views, search, filters, selected-state display and group-add confirmation to Dash. Use the supported catalogue and workspace APIs only.
Acceptance criteria: Users can inspect every Public Skill; group confirmation shows the atomic Skills to be added; unavailable Skills are clear; workspace changes are visible without affecting active Goals.

Story: Support mechanically validated Private Skills
Outcome: Allow a user to create a private Skill that uses only approved read-only capabilities.
Implementation notes: Create submission, schema validation, capability allowlisting, ownership and immutable version records. Reject any write-capable or unavailable capability. Keep provider endpoints centrally managed.
Acceptance criteria: A private Skill is visible only to its owner; validation is deterministic; it cannot introduce endpoints or write capabilities; versions used by active Goals remain stable.

Story: Add reviewed Public and team Skill publication
Outcome: Support governed reuse beyond private Skills.
Implementation notes: Add review states, reviewer decisions and immutable publication for Public Skills. Add team-aligned visibility when organisational group data is available.
Acceptance criteria: Public publication always requires approval; authors cannot approve their own version; team visibility is enforced centrally; publication does not mutate versions already used by active Goals.

Story: Define the delegated identity header contract
Outcome: Standardise the trusted context that an MCP security shim receives.
Implementation notes: Define signed or otherwise trusted user, workspace, environment and correlation context; specify header stripping, forwarding, expiry and consistent denial responses.
Acceptance criteria: Untrusted callers cannot forge context; every field has a source and lifetime; denial responses have stable codes; the contract contains no provider-specific assumptions.

Story: Build the reusable MCP security shim
Outcome: Front vendor MCP servers with a configurable component that enforces the trusted header contract.
Implementation notes: Create a deployable template that validates context, removes caller-supplied identity headers, maps identity to provider credentials or delegated access and proxies MCP traffic. Keep the adapter interface provider-specific but the core reusable.
Acceptance criteria: The shim fronts a reference MCP server; forged headers are rejected; correlation passes through; provider denial is normalised; deployment documentation covers configuration and health checks.

Story: Implement platform-specific delegated RBAC adapters
Outcome: Apply namespace, tablespace or equivalent platform boundaries at every provider call.
Implementation notes: Implement and test adapters for the first selected platforms. Forward the correct credential or scope to the provider and return a consistent denial envelope to MOSAIC.
Acceptance criteria: Authorised data is returned; cross-boundary access is denied by the provider path; MOSAIC does not duplicate provider RBAC; tests cover expired, absent and insufficient delegated identity.

Story: Create the relational Integration registry
Outcome: Replace file-only provider, target, capability and binding definitions with normalised versioned records.
Implementation notes: Add SQLAlchemy models and Alembic migrations for Providers, Targets, Capabilities, Bindings and immutable publications. Preserve the terminology and validation rules from the runtime contract.
Acceptance criteria: Relations enforce referential integrity; draft changes do not affect active publications; each publication has a stable snapshot ID; retention settings can identify removable old publications.

Story: Publish validated runtime configuration from the registry
Outcome: Generate the orchestrator's existing runtime representation directly from approved database records at startup.
Implementation notes: Validate a complete draft, publish it immutably, and reconstruct the runtime model in memory when MOSAIC starts. Do not persist a JSON document in PostgreSQL as the strategic runtime source.
Acceptance criteria: Every replica reconstructs the same publication by snapshot ID; invalid drafts cannot publish; startup fails closed on inconsistent data; the GCS JSON path can be disabled after cutover.

Story: Retain and clean old Integration publications
Outcome: Prevent unlimited version growth while preserving governed rollback windows.
Implementation notes: Add configurable retention by count or age, protect active and explicitly retained publications, and provide a safe administrative cleanup command with dry-run output.
Acceptance criteria: Protected publications are never removed; cleanup reports exact targets; active replicas continue using their loaded publication; retention can be disabled.

Story: Create the standalone Integration workbench
Outcome: Provide a separate application for viewing and editing provider, target, capability and binding definitions.
Implementation notes: Deploy the workbench independently from the MOSAIC runtime. Reuse production identity and registry APIs. Permit deep links from MOSAIC without coupling runtime availability to the workbench.
Acceptance criteria: The workbench can be deployed and upgraded separately; runtime continues when it is unavailable; users cannot bypass registry permissions; deep links resolve to stable records.

Story: Visualise and validate binding relationships
Outcome: Make capability-to-provider-tool and target routing relationships understandable before publication.
Implementation notes: Add graph and table views, draft editing, argument mapping, result extraction, limits and validation output. Highlight missing and conflicting relationships.
Acceptance criteria: A reviewer can trace each capability to its provider tool and target routing; validation errors identify exact fields; read-only and safety limits are visible; large configurations remain navigable.

Story: Publish approved Integration drafts
Outcome: Complete the governed authoring workflow without direct database or JSON editing.
Implementation notes: Add review, approval and immutable publication actions using registry APIs. Record actor, timestamp and validation result. Prevent authors from bypassing required approval policy.
Acceptance criteria: Only a valid approved draft can publish; publication returns a snapshot ID; audit history is queryable; failed publication leaves the active snapshot unchanged.

Story: Add configurable conversation retention
Outcome: Expire inactive conversations without requiring whole-database deletion.
Implementation notes: Implement a scheduled retention process based on last activity, with dry-run, configurable duration and disabled mode. Keep workspace metadata independent.
Acceptance criteria: Expired sessions are removed according to policy; disabled mode retains them; active sessions are protected; cleanup metrics and exact counts are logged.

Story: Add production request and concurrency limits
Outcome: Protect shared capacity with explicit, measurable behaviour.
Implementation notes: Implement configured per-user and platform limits using shared storage. Return 429 with the exact limit, reset time or retry condition. Keep the existing per-conversation 409 guard.
Acceptance criteria: Limits are documented and observable; responses never say only 'try shortly'; multiple replicas enforce the same counters; administrators can change limits without code changes.

Story: Add usage attribution and chargeback records
Outcome: Attribute model consumption to the correct user or service when ADA telemetry is not sufficiently granular.
Implementation notes: Consume approved ADA/GCP usage records and map them to trusted MOSAIC identity and invocation IDs. Persist only the minimal ledger required for reporting and reconciliation.
Acceptance criteria: Usage totals reconcile to the source telemetry; human and service identities are distinct; prompts and capability evidence are excluded; retention and access controls are documented.

Story: Add production backup, recovery and alerting
Outcome: Meet agreed production recovery and support targets.
Implementation notes: Back up PostgreSQL, test restore, add service-level dashboards and alert on availability, error rate, database capacity and invocation failures.
Acceptance criteria: Restore meets the approved recovery targets; alerts have owners and runbooks; dashboards separate user errors from platform failures; restore exercises are repeatable.
Dependencies: Release 1 Cloud SQL foundation; production SLOs

Story: Handle explicit mid-Goal topic changes
Outcome: Let a user abandon a clarification-held Goal and start a different Goal deliberately.
Implementation notes: Add an explicit transition that closes the current Goal as abandoned, keeps its raw evidence isolated and starts a new Goal using the current workspace Skills. Do not infer topic change solely from model text.
Acceptance criteria: The user confirms abandonment; the old Goal cannot resume; its raw outcomes cannot satisfy the new Goal; conversation history remains available; the transition is auditable.
